newsitem.title: BOSNIA: EU quietly ends peace mission in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: EU quietly ends peace mission in Mostar.

text.p: The European Union's mandate to administer the Bosnian city of Mostar will quietly expire at midnight on New Year's eve after more than two years of diplomacy failed to ease the city's strict ethnic division.

International High Representative to Bosnia Carl Bildt will take over supervision of the peace process in Mostar and the surrounding region from January 1. But officials say the High Representive's mission is less ambitious and not seen as a successor to the EU. EU envoys first arrived in Mostar in 1994 shortly after Bosnian Moslems and Croats signed a ceasefire ending a bitter 10-month war that devastated the city.

EU officials had vowed to prevent Mostar from turning into another Berlin but the goal of reuniting the town is still far away despite an infusion of 270 million German marks ($180 million) in reconstruction aid.
Sir Martin Garrod, the outgoing EU envoy to Mostar, gave the EU mission high marks for an array of reconstruction projects that helped restore the city's infrastructure.
But he said political progress on forming a unified government and police force has been slow.
"The more difficult part was on the political side," Garrod told Reuters by telephone.
An inter-ethnic municipal government, elected in June, is in place but remains bogged down in political infighting.
U.N. human rights workers say gangsters still rule in the western sector and promises from their patrons in Croatia to remove them have never been fulfilled.
Ordinary people live in ethnic ghettoes, afraid of crossing former front lines.
Since the Bosnian war ended a year ago, the remaining Moslems from the Croat-held western side have been systematically expelled.
"I would feel much happier if the climate of fear and intimidation in Mostar could be eliminated," Garrod said.
He said the climate made people afraid to express their opinions openly and allowed evictions to continue.
"Only until all leaders are willing to stand up and speak out against this intimidation will it end."
Garrod said it was naiive to expect a quick reconciliation after the vicious fighting that took place in Mostar, which had a mixed population of Moslems, Croats and Serbs before the war.
Similar conflicts in Spain and other European countries have left scars for years, he added.
"The wounds are very deep...We are getting frustrated after three years that people are not shaking hands and living happily ever after. It's going to take time."
Political developments in Croatia, where President Franjo Tudjman, according to some reports is seriously ill, could end up playing a crucial role in determining Mostar's future, Garrod said.
"Zagreb has always had a powerful effect on Mostar," he said. "The poor health of the president is a significant factor we will have to see how things develop."
